author: Carlos Martinez
title: Pre-race nerves in iRacing: manage anxiety before green flag
description: Practical techniques to calm nerves, control breathing, and stabilize mental state in the minutes before an iRacing race.

sections.p: Nerves before an iRacing race are real, even though no physical stakes exist. Your heart rate climbs, focus fragments, and muscle tension rises. The brain treats reputation loss and lost iRating the same way it treats physical threat. That nervous system response floods your body with cortisol and adrenaline, which degrades fine motor control, narrows peripheral awareness, and scrambles short-term memory. A calm driver hits apexes cleanly and reads traffic. A wired driver locks the brakes and runs off track on lap two.

The gap between your base pace and nerve-affected pace can be half a second or more. That margin exists in every race you enter. The drivers who close it are the ones who build a pre-race routine that works for them. This is not mental weakness. It is preparation.

Your nervous system has two manual controls: breathing and body position. Breathing is the fastest one to use. A sympathetic (fight-or-flight) state produces rapid, shallow chest breathing. A parasympathetic (calm) state produces slow, deep diaphragmatic breathing. You can flip states by changing your breath pattern.

Start five minutes before the race. Breathe in through your nose for a count of four. Hold for a count of four. Exhale through your mouth for a count of six. The long exhale is the key. It signals safety to your vagus nerve, which is the main parasympathetic highway. Repeat this cycle ten times. Your heart rate will drop measurably within two minutes.

list: Breathe in for four counts, hold for four, exhale for six (repeat 10 times)
Do this seated in your rig or away from the monitor
Perform it again once you are loaded into the grid, if the client allows it
Return to normal breathing once the race starts; this is a reset, not a technique to hold during racing

sections.p: Anxiety lives in a future that hasn't happened yet. Your body lives in the present. Grounding techniques pull your mind into the present moment by engaging your senses.

One minute before the race loads, do a body scan. Start at your toes and mentally touch each part: toes, feet, calves, thighs, hips, stomach, chest, shoulders, arms, hands, neck, head. Feel the seat under you. Feel the wheel in your hands. Feel the pedals under your feet. Notice the temperature of the air. Listen to your fans or speakers. This takes 60 seconds and anchors you in the rig, not in the imagined future.
Another approach: press your feet hard into the floor. Hold for five seconds. Release. Do this three times. The physical exertion converts nervous energy into a grounded state.
Pre-race nerves generate automatic thoughts. Most are worst-case stories. You will spin. You will crash. You will DNF. You will lose iRating. These stories feel like predictions, but they are habits.

Replace them. Five minutes before the race, state three facts about your preparation. Not wishes. Facts. Examples: "I ran this track five times in practice and hit my target pace." "My setup matches my driving style." "I have no mechanical issues with my rig." These anchor you in what is true, not what might go wrong.

During the race, replace panicked self-talk with single-word or two-word commands. "Smooth." "Late apex." "Smooth braking." "Check mirrors." These interrupt spiraling thoughts and redirect your brain toward the next immediate action, not the race outcome.

list: State three factual statements about your preparation (not hopes or fears)
Use simple two-word commands during the race to refocus your attention
Avoid outcome language ("I need to stay ahead") and use action language ("Turn in smooth")

sections.p: The warm-up lap is free laps before the race begins. Use it to settle your nervous system and dial in your inputs, not to push for a hot lap.

The first lap should feel easy. Purposely underdrive it. Let your muscle memory find the line without pressure. This teaches your body that the track is familiar and safe. The second lap can lift to 85 percent of your target pace. The third lap can reach 95 percent. By the time you cross the line into the race, your body has practiced the motion dozens of times in a low-threat context. Nerves drop because the motion is now routine.

sections.tip: Do not use the warm-up lap to find setup gains or validate your pace against the pole. Use it to calm your nervous system through repetition.

sections.p: What you hear and see shapes your emotional state. A busy practice lobby full of liveries and car names generates low-level stress. Your brain is processing dozens of competitive signals. Close the spotter app or minimize it. Mute team radio or other chat. Dim overhead lights if you race in daylight. Create sensory neutrality.

Some drivers play calm music (lo-fi, ambient, instrumental). Others prefer silence. Test both and see which one settles your mind. If you do play music, start it ten minutes before the race, not thirty seconds before. Your brain needs time to integrate it into a calm state, not start absorbing it during the anxiety peak.
Build a repeatable routine and use it before every race. Consistency is the goal. Your nervous system learns the pattern and begins to associate it with safety.

olist: 15 minutes before: close unnecessary windows, put phone in another room, dim lights, start calm music if you use it
10 minutes before: use the breathing technique (4-4-6, ten cycles)
5 minutes before: do the body scan or foot press grounding exercise
3 minutes before: state your three factual preparation statements
1 minute before: load into the race, take three final deep breaths
On grid: allow the warm-up lap to settle your inputs through repetition

sections.p: This routine takes about 15 minutes total and requires no special equipment. You need only the rig you already have and the ability to close your eyes for 60 seconds. The science behind each step (parasympathetic activation via breath, grounding via sensation, narrative control via self-talk, and practice via warm-up) is robust. The drivers who use it consistently report that their first-lap pace is closer to their practice pace, that they recover faster from mistakes, and that they finish more races instead of binning it in the first five laps.
You are not trying to eliminate nerves. Some activation improves focus and reaction time. The goal is to drop it from panic into confidence. The difference is breath control and presence.

faqs.q: Can I use the breathing technique during a race?
faqs.a: No. The 4-4-6 breathing is a reset tool for before the race. During the race, breathe normally and focus on smooth inputs and reading traffic. The warm-up lap and pre-race routine have already settled your nervous system by the time green flag drops.

faqs.q: What if my rig is in a noisy or bright room?
faqs.a: Close the door to your sim space if you can, or hang a blanket over a window to reduce ambient light. Use noise-canceling headphones or loop rain or wind audio if music feels wrong. Even small reductions in sensory noise help. If your environment is very chaotic, move your race to a quieter time of day if possible.

faqs.q: Does this routine work if I am already salty from a bad previous race?
faqs.a: The technique works best when you use it consistently, not just when you are already upset. If you race back-to-back and the first one went badly, the breathing and grounding still help reset your state before the second race, but do not expect magic. Take a 10-minute break between races if you can. Walk away from the rig, hydrate, and step outside. Your nervous system needs recovery time, not just a breathing drill.

faqs.q: Should I do this routine before practice sessions too, or only races?
faqs.a: Practice sessions do not carry the same emotional weight, so the routine is less critical. If you are testing a new car or practicing a track for the first time, a quick 4-4-6 breathing is still useful to clear your mind before you start. Reserve the full 15-minute routine for official races and league events where your iRating or reputation is on the line.
